title: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
summary: When can a node removed from a lock-free structure be freed? Hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation and RCU grace periods, their exact rules, worked numbers and the read-cost versus bounded-garbage tradeoff.
outcomes: Explain why freeing a node right after unlinking it is a use-after-free, even with tagged pointers
Trace the hazard pointer publish, fence, validate loop and a Scan, and compute the N x R garbage bound
Apply the epoch rules to decide when retired garbage may be freed, and why one stalled thread blocks it
Use the RCU API correctly and explain which readers a grace period waits for
Choose between RCU, EBR and hazard pointers from read pattern, preemption and memory limits

lessons.title: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part

blocks.md:
Recall the Treiber stack from the ABA course: `pop` loads `top`, reads `top->next`, then uses compare-and-swap (CAS) to swing `top` to that next node. Getting a node *out* of the structure is solved. This course is about the step after that: when may the thread that popped node A call `free(A)`?

The trouble is that other threads may have loaded the address of A a moment earlier and are about to read it. They hold a **private reference**: the address sits in a register or local variable, invisible to everyone else.

blocks.title: Freeing a popped node while another thread still reads it

scenes.caption: T1 starts a pop and loads top. It now holds the address of node A in a local variable, but has not read A yet.
T2 pops A first. Its CAS succeeds, so A is unlinked: no shared pointer leads to A any more. T2 believes it owns A and frees it.
T1 resumes and reads the next field of A. A is freed memory: this is a use-after-free. The page may even have been returned to the OS, so the read can crash.
Worse, the allocator can hand A's memory to a new push. Now T1's CAS compares against the same address A and can succeed with a stale next pointer: the ABA problem from the previous course.

add.label: CAS top A to a stale next

blocks.md:
Three words will be used precisely from now on:

- **Remove** (or unlink): make the node unreachable from shared memory. New operations can no longer find it.
- **Retire**: hand the removed node to a reclamation scheme, saying "free this when it is safe".
- **Reclaim**: actually free or reuse the memory.

The whole subject is the gap between retire and reclaim. A removed node is *safe to reclaim* only once no thread can still hold a private reference obtained before the removal. Threads that start later cannot find the node, so they never matter.

blocks.prompt: Tagged pointers (a version counter next to the pointer) fixed ABA in the previous course. Do they also make `free(A)` right after the pop safe?
blocks.reveal: No. The tag makes T1's final CAS fail, which fixes ABA. But T1 still *reads* `A->next` before that CAS, and that read touches freed memory. If the allocator unmapped the page, the read faults; if it reused the block, T1 computes with garbage. Tagged pointers are only safe when nodes are never returned to the general allocator (for example a type-stable free list). Reclamation needs a separate mechanism.

blocks.md:
The obvious fixes all fail:

- **Never free.** No crash, but memory grows without bound in a long-running server.
- **Free immediately.** The bug above.
- **Reference count each node.** Every traversed node's counter must be incremented and decremented, even by read-only operations, so readers write to shared cache lines. Valois's lock-free version also never lets a node change type, so memory cannot go back to the OS. In Michael's hash-table test (load factor 5, four processors) hazard pointers delivered 573 percent of the reference-counting throughput.

So practical schemes avoid per-node counts and answer one question cheaply: *has every thread that might hold a reference to this retired node moved on?*

There are two families of answers, and the rest of the course covers both:

1. **Track pointers.** Each reader publicly announces the exact few nodes it is using. A retired node is freed when no announcement matches it. This is **hazard pointers** (Michael, 2004).
2. **Track time.** Readers announce only *that* they are inside an operation. A retired node is freed after every operation that was running at retire time has ended, a span called a **grace period**. This covers **epoch-based reclamation** (Fraser, 2004) and **RCU** in the Linux kernel.

A garbage collector does not make ABA impossible in every case. Michael points out that if a program moves the same live node back and forth between two lists, ABA can still occur even with perfect GC. What a GC (and the schemes in this course) guarantees is narrower: a node's address is not reused while someone can still reach it.
Removing a node and freeing it are different events. Every scheme in this course defers the free until no thread can still hold a reference taken before the removal.

blocks.question: T2 pops node A from a lock-free stack and calls `free(A)` immediately. T1 had loaded `top == A` just before. Which statement is correct?
options: It is safe because T1's CAS will fail when it sees that top changed
It is safe if the stack uses tagged pointers
It is unsafe because T1 will dereference A to read its next field, even if its later CAS would fail
It is unsafe only on weakly ordered CPUs such as ARM
blocks.explain: The CAS comes last. Before it, T1 reads `A->next`, which touches freed memory. A failing CAS or a tag check cannot undo a read that already happened. This is independent of the CPU memory model: it is a use-after-free in program order.

blocks.question: Which threads can possibly hold a reference to a node that was unlinked at time t?
options: Any thread that will run in the future
Only threads whose current operation started before t and is still running
Only the thread that unlinked it
No thread, because unlinking is atomic
blocks.explain: After the unlink, the node is unreachable from shared memory, so an operation starting later cannot find it. Only operations already in progress at time t may have loaded its address. Every scheme here is a way to detect when those operations have finished, or that they do not point at this node.

lessons.title: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading

blocks.md:
Maged Michael's **hazard pointers** (IEEE TPDS, 2004) give each thread a few shared, single-writer pointer slots. A **hazard pointer** holds the address of a node its owner is about to dereference. Only the owner writes its slots; every thread may read them.

The rule, as the C++26 proposal states it: a retired object can be reclaimed only after it is determined that no hazard pointer has been pointing to it *continuously from a time before its retirement*. With $N$ threads and $K$ hazard pointers each there are $H = NK$ slots in total. A stack needs $K=1$; queues and linked lists need $K=2$.

Setting a hazard pointer is not enough on its own. Between loading `top` and publishing it, another thread may already have unlinked, retired and scanned past the node. So the reader **publishes, then validates**: after writing the slot it re-reads the source pointer. If the source still points to the node, the node was still in the structure *after* the hazard pointer became visible, so any later scan will see the slot. If not, it retries.

The publish must become visible before the re-read. That is a store followed by a load, an ordering that even x86 may reorder, so a full fence goes between them. Hart et al. point out the cost: one fence per visited node.

blocks.title: Treiber stack pop with one hazard pointer

scenes.caption: Thread T0 loads top and gets node A. The address is only private so far: nothing stops another thread from freeing A.
T0 publishes A in its hazard pointer slot, then fences so the slot is globally visible before the next load.
Meanwhile T1 popped A and retired it. T0's reload sees top == B, so validation fails. T0 never touched A, and it retries.
Second attempt: T0 loads B, publishes B, fences, and validation succeeds. From here on B cannot be reclaimed, so reading the next field of B is safe.
The CAS swings top from B to C. T0 copies the data out, clears its slot and calls retire(B) instead of free(B). B will be freed by a later scan once no slot holds it.

blocks.md:
Retiring is cheap. Each thread keeps a private **retired list**. When its length reaches a threshold $R$, the thread runs **Scan**:

1. Read every hazard pointer slot and collect the non-null values into a private set (Michael recommends a sorted array searched by binary search, or a hash table).
2. For each node in the retired list: if its address is not in the set, free it; otherwise keep it for the next scan.

Scan uses only ordinary reads of the slots, so it is wait-free.

blocks.title: One Scan by T0: 3 threads, K = 2, R = 8

scenes.caption: T0 has retired 8 nodes, reaching R = 8, so it scans. There are H = 3 x 2 = 6 hazard slots; T1 is protecting n3 and n7, T2 is protecting n5.
Stage 1: copy the non-null slots into a private set {n3, n5, n7}. The slots are read once; threads may change them during the scan without breaking safety.
Stage 2: look up each retired node. n3, n5 and n7 are in the set, so they stay in the list. The other 5 nodes have no hazard pointer and are freed.
After the scan T0's list holds 3 nodes. Since at most H = 6 slots can match, every scan of R = 8 nodes frees at least R minus H = 2, and here it freed 5.

blocks.md:
Michael's analysis gives the two numbers that make the scheme practical:

- **Amortized constant cost.** If $R = H + \Omega(H)$, for example $R = 2H$, each scan does $O(R)$ expected work and frees at least $R - H$ nodes, which is $\Omega(R)$. So each retired node costs $O(1)$ amortized.
- **Bounded garbage.** Each thread holds at most $R$ retired nodes, so at most $NR$ retired nodes are ever waiting, *even if some threads are delayed or have crashed*. With $N=4$, $K=2$, $H=8$ and $R=16$ that is 64 nodes.

blocks.tex: \text{work per freed node} \le \frac{H + R}{R - H}, \qquad \text{garbage} \le N R
blocks.caption: Simplified cost model: a scan reads H slots and looks up R nodes, and frees at least R minus H of them.

scenes.caption: With H = 8 and R = 9, a scan may free only 1 node, so the worst case is 17 units of work per freed node. R barely above H wastes scans.
At R = 2H = 16 the bound drops to 3, and R = 32 gives about 1.67. Beyond 2H the gains are small, while the garbage bound N x R keeps growing linearly.
More threads means more slots: at H = 16 the same curve shifts right, so R must grow with the thread count to stay amortized.

blocks.prompt: A reader is preempted for 10 seconds while holding a hazard pointer to node X. Other threads keep popping and retiring nodes at full speed. How much unreclaimed memory piles up?
blocks.reveal: Only X stays pinned. Every other retired node has no matching slot and is freed at the next scan, so the waiting garbage stays below $NR$ no matter how long the reader sleeps. This robustness to stalled threads is what sets hazard pointers apart from the grace-period schemes in the next lessons.

blocks.md: The per-node fence is the main read-side cost. Folly's production implementation (the reference for C++26 `std::hazard_pointer`) uses an *asymmetric* fence: on Linux the reader side is only a compiler barrier, and the scanner pays instead with a heavy process-wide barrier (`membarrier`). The C++26 proposal reports protection under one nanosecond with a pre-constructed hazard pointer.
Hazard pointers: publish the address, fence, re-validate, then dereference. Retire into a private list and scan when it reaches R. Garbage is bounded by N x R even if threads stall.

blocks.question: A developer removes the re-validation step: after `hp[me] = t; full_fence();` the code reads `t->next` directly. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the fence already makes the hazard pointer visible
Another thread may have retired and freed t before the hazard pointer was published, so reading its next field touches freed memory
The CAS will always fail
The retired list will grow without bound
blocks.explain: Publishing only protects a node that is still in the structure at the moment the slot becomes visible. If t was unlinked and a scan ran between the load and the publish, the scan saw no slot and freed t. The re-read proves t was still reachable after the publish, so every later scan must see the slot.

blocks.question: N = 8 threads, K = 2 hazard pointers each, R = 2H. What is the maximum number of retired-but-unfreed nodes, and the minimum freed per scan?
options: 16 and 8
32 and 16
128 and 8
blocks.explain: H = N x K = 16, so R = 32. The bound is N x R = 8 x 32 = 256 waiting nodes. Each scan checks 32 nodes and at most 16 can be protected, so it frees at least R minus H = 16.

lessons.title: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later

blocks.md:
Hazard pointers track *which* nodes each reader holds. Keir Fraser's **epoch-based reclamation** (EBR), from his 2004 Cambridge thesis, tracks only *when* each reader started. It builds on older "limbo list" designs (Kung and Lehman, 1980).

The idea: a retired node is already unreachable, so the only threads that can reference it are those whose operation started before it was retired. If we know every thread has started a fresh operation since then, the node is safe. EBR detects this with a single global counter, the **epoch**.

The rules, in the form used by Rust's `crossbeam-epoch`:

1. **Pin.** Before touching shared nodes, a thread enters a critical section by copying the global epoch into its own slot and marking itself pinned. On exit it unpins.
2. **Retire.** Unlinked nodes go into garbage tagged with the current global epoch.
3. **Advance.** Any thread may move the global epoch from $e$ to $e+1$, but only if every *pinned* thread is pinned in epoch $e$. Unpinned threads never block it.
4. **Free.** Garbage tagged $b$ is freed once the global epoch is at least $b + 2$.

scenes.caption: Start: global epoch 0, no thread pinned, no garbage. Garbage will be tagged with the epoch in which it was retired.
T0 and T1 pin, recording epoch 0. T1 pops node A and retires it: A goes into the garbage tagged 0. T0 might still hold A, so A must wait.
T1 unpins. T2 pins at 0 and tries to advance: every pinned thread (T0, T2) is in epoch 0, so the global epoch becomes 1. Nothing is old enough to free yet.
T1 pins again, now recording epoch 1, and retires B and C, tagged 1. Pinned threads are now spread over epochs 0 and 1, which is the most spread the rule allows.
T1 tries to advance to 2 and fails: T0 and T2 are still pinned in epoch 0. They might hold A, B or C, so nothing is freed.
T0 and T2 finish and unpin. T1, the only pinned thread, is in epoch 1, so the epoch advances to 2. A was tagged 0 and 2 minus 0 is 2, so A is freed.
T0 pins at 2. T1 repins at 2 and retires D (tag 2). Both pinned threads are in epoch 2, so the epoch advances to 3 and B and C (tag 1) are freed.
Now T0 is descheduled while pinned. T1 repins at 3, retires E, F and H, and fails to advance. Until T0 runs again, nothing tagged 2 or later can ever be freed.

blocks.prompt: Why wait until the epoch reaches b + 2? When the epoch first moves past b to b + 1, are the nodes tagged b not already safe?
blocks.reveal: Not yet. Rule 3 only requires pinned threads to be in the *current* epoch, so at the moment the epoch becomes $b+1$ some threads are still pinned in $b$, and they may have loaded a node retired in $b$. As crossbeam's source puts it, a pinned thread can witness at most one epoch advance. The advance to $b+2$ requires every pinned thread to be in $b+1$, so all critical sections from epoch $b$ have ended. Fraser notes this is why only three limbo lists are ever needed: $e$, $e-1$ and the one being freed.

blocks.md:
Reading is now cheap: pinning happens once per *operation*, not once per node, so a traversal of 1000 nodes pays the same as a traversal of 1. Hart et al. count two fences per operation, one on entry and one on exit, against one per visited node for hazard pointers.

The price is in the last scene. Fraser is explicit that the scheme is *not strictly lock-free*: a process that stalls inside an operation never observes later epochs, "the limbo lists will never be reclaimed and memory cannot be reused." Preemption is enough to cause this.

blocks.caption: A Treiber stack pop with crossbeam-epoch. `pin()` returns a Guard; `defer_destroy` retires the node. Compare with the hazard pointer version: no per-node publish or validate.

blocks.md:
crossbeam-epoch adds engineering on top of Fraser's rules (from its `internal.rs`):

- Retired objects first go into a thread-local **bag** of up to 64 deferred functions, so most retires touch no shared memory. A full bag is sealed with the current global epoch and pushed onto a global queue.
- Every 128th pin, the thread tries to advance the epoch and destroys up to 8 expired bags, so no background collector thread is needed.
- A bag is expired when the global epoch minus its tag is at least 2, which is rule 4.

Holding a guard is holding back everyone's garbage. Pinning across a blocking call, a lock wait or a long iteration stops the epoch from advancing for all threads. crossbeam provides `Guard::repin` to briefly unpin and pin again inside long loops; references loaded before the repin are no longer protected.
EBR pays per operation, not per node, and needs no per-node announcement. In exchange, a single thread stalled while pinned blocks all reclamation, so garbage is unbounded.

blocks.question: Thread T is pinned in epoch 5 and stays pinned. What is the highest value the global epoch can reach?
options: Unbounded, since other threads keep advancing
blocks.explain: Advancing from 5 to 6 is allowed because T is pinned in 5, the current epoch. Advancing from 6 to 7 requires every pinned thread to be in 6, and T is still in 5. So the epoch stops at 6, and garbage tagged 5 or later (freeable at 7 or later) piles up.

blocks.question: A request handler calls `epoch::pin()`, reads a node from a lock-free map, then makes a 2-second network call before dropping the guard. What is the main problem?
options: The node may be freed during the network call
The network call will deadlock
No memory retired by any thread during those 2 seconds can be reclaimed
The guard will be dropped automatically after 128 pins
blocks.explain: The node is safe; the guard guarantees that. The cost lands on everyone else: the pinned thread keeps the global epoch from advancing past its epoch plus one, so all garbage retired meanwhile waits. Copy what you need, drop the guard, then do the slow call.

lessons.title: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period

blocks.md:
**RCU** (read-copy update) is the Linux kernel's answer, added during 2.5 development and tuned for read-mostly data. The kernel documentation splits every update into two phases:

- **Removal**: replace or remove pointers so that new readers cannot reach the old data. This runs concurrently with readers.
- **Reclamation**: free the old data, but only after every reader that was active during removal has finished.

The wait in between is the **grace period**. It is the same idea as EBR's two epochs, and Fraser himself notes that RCU applies limbo lists to the Linux kernel.

blocks.title: Read, copy, update on a single global pointer

scenes.caption: Reader 1 is inside rcu_read_lock() and has fetched gbl_foo with rcu_dereference(). It is reading the only version, where a = 1.
The updater allocates a new struct, copies the old one into it and changes a. Nobody can see the copy yet, so no reader is disturbed.
rcu_assign_pointer() publishes the copy with a release store: one aligned pointer write. Reader 2 now finds the new version; reader 1 keeps the old. Both are valid at once.
synchronize_rcu() waits for every read-side critical section that began before the publish. Reader 1 finishes. Reader 2 started later and cannot reach old, so it is not waited for.
The grace period is over, so no reader can hold old. kfree(old_fp) is now safe. Only one version remains.

blocks.md:
The core API has five calls:

- `rcu_read_lock()` and `rcu_read_unlock()` bracket a **read-side critical section**. Blocking inside one is illegal (preemptible kernels may preempt it).
- `rcu_dereference(p)` loads a protected pointer for later use inside the section.
- `rcu_assign_pointer(p, v)` publishes with store-release ordering, so the new struct's fields are initialized before any reader can see the pointer.
- `synchronize_rcu()` blocks until all *pre-existing* read-side critical sections complete. `call_rcu()` is the non-blocking form: it queues a callback to run after the grace period, and `kfree_rcu()` is the shortcut when the callback only frees.

blocks.caption: Adapted from the kernel's whatisRCU.rst. The reader takes no lock and makes no shared write; the updater copies, publishes, waits, then frees.

blocks.title: synchronize_rcu() waits only for pre-existing readers

scenes.caption: Step 1: CPU 0 enters an RCU read-side critical section with rcu_read_lock().
Step 2: CPU 1 has removed an item and enters synchronize_rcu(). CPU 0's reader is pre-existing, so it must be waited for.
Step 3: CPU 2 starts a new reader. It began after the removal, so it cannot find the removed item, and synchronize_rcu() does not wait for it.
Step 4: CPU 0 calls rcu_read_unlock(). Every pre-existing reader is done, so the grace period can end.
Step 5: synchronize_rcu() returns, possibly a little later than step 4 because of batching, and CPU 1 frees the item. Step 6: CPU 2's reader ends whenever it likes.

blocks.md:
How can the reclaimer know readers are done if `rcu_read_lock()` writes nothing? The documentation's "classic RCU" toy answers it. In a non-preemptive kernel, `rcu_read_lock()` and `rcu_read_unlock()` compile to *nothing*, and `synchronize_rcu()` just runs itself on each CPU in turn. Since blocking in a read-side section is illegal, a CPU that has context-switched has finished all its earlier read-side sections.

A point where a thread holds no references, such as a context switch, is a **quiescent state**. Hart et al. call this family **quiescent-state-based reclamation** (QSBR). It has zero read-side fences, the cheapest reads of any scheme.

RCU protects readers from updaters, not updaters from each other. `rcu_assign_pointer()` does not make two concurrent updates safe; the example still takes `foo_mutex`. And a pointer from `rcu_dereference()` is valid only inside the critical section that fetched it.

Outside the kernel, the same model is available as **liburcu**, a userspace RCU library by Mathieu Desnoyers and Paul McKenney used by projects such as Knot DNS and BIND, and as the C++26 `<rcu>` header (proposal P2545). There a reader writes `std::scoped_lock l(std::rcu_default_domain());`, an object derived from `std::rcu_obj_base` is retired with `retire()`, and `std::rcu_synchronize()` waits for a grace period.

RCU readers pay almost nothing; updaters copy, publish with one pointer store, and defer the free until a grace period has elapsed. A grace period waits only for readers that started before the removal.

blocks.question:
Spot the bug:
`rcu_read_lock(); p = rcu_dereference(head.next); rcu_read_unlock(); x = p->data;`
options: rcu_dereference should be rcu_assign_pointer
p->data is read after rcu_read_unlock, so a grace period may have ended and p may be freed
rcu_read_lock cannot be called on head.next
There is no bug because readers never block
blocks.explain: Once the critical section ends, the reader no longer delays grace periods, so an updater's synchronize_rcu() can return and kfree(p). The kernel documentation shows exactly this pattern marked BUG. Read p->data before rcu_read_unlock(), or take a reference count to keep it longer.

blocks.question: CPU 1 calls synchronize_rcu() at time 10. Reader X started at time 8 and ends at 12; reader Y starts at 11 and ends at 30. Ignoring batching delays, when may synchronize_rcu() return?
options: At 30, after both readers
At 10, immediately, because readers take no locks
At 12, after X; Y need not be waited for
At 11, when Y starts
blocks.explain: Only pre-existing read-side critical sections count. X was running at time 10, so the grace period must cover it. Y started after the removal and cannot have obtained the removed pointer, so waiting for it would be wasted. Real implementations may return somewhat later because they batch requests.

lessons.title: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage

blocks.md:
Hart, McKenney and Brown ran the first side-by-side comparison of these schemes (IPDPS 2006) and concluded that **there is no globally optimal scheme**. Two axes decide the choice:

- **Read-side cost**: what a reader pays per operation and per node it visits.
- **Robustness**: how much garbage can pile up when a thread is slow, preempted or dead.

blocks.title: Fences per lookup in a list, by nodes visited

scenes.caption: Visiting 1 node: hazard pointers need one fence (publish then validate), EBR two (pin and unpin), QSBR none. Simplified count from Hart et al.; it ignores the CAS of updates.
Visiting 5 nodes: hazard pointers pay a fence per node, so 5. EBR still pays 2 per operation, QSBR still 0.
Visiting 20 nodes: 20 fences against 2. On Hart et al.'s 2006 machines a fence cost about 76 to 78 ns, so that is roughly 1520 ns of fences against 152 ns.

blocks.md:
Hart et al. measured exactly this shape: per-element fences degrade hazard pointers on long traversals, while QSBR and EBR do much better, and QSBR is cheapest in the base case. Update-heavy workloads flip part of the picture, because every hazard-pointer scan must search the hazard array.

The second axis goes the other way. Michael proves hazard pointers keep at most $NR$ retired nodes waiting, even when threads are delayed or crashed. Grace-period schemes have no such bound: one thread stalled inside a critical section stops every free.

blocks.title: Garbage waiting while one reader is stalled

scenes.caption: Simplified model: the other threads keep retiring 10 nodes per ms. With grace periods, nothing retired after the stall can be freed, so the backlog grows linearly: 1000 nodes after 100 ms.
With hazard pointers only the stalled reader's own protected node stays. Each thread holds at most R retired nodes, so the backlog flattens at N x R = 64 after 6.4 ms.
Raising R to 64 with 8 threads lifts the cap to N x R = 512, reached after 51.2 ms. This is the tradeoff from lesson 2: larger R means cheaper scans but more memory held.

blocks.md:
Putting it together:

- **RCU / QSBR**: near-zero read cost, but it needs natural quiescent states (the kernel has context switches) and reclamation stalls with any stuck reader. Updaters must still synchronize with each other. Best for read-mostly data such as lookup tables or configuration.
- **EBR** (crossbeam-epoch): automatic, cheap per operation, invisible to the programmer. Unbounded garbage if a pinned thread stalls.
- **Hazard pointers** (Folly, C++26 `<hazard_pointer>`): bounded garbage and tolerant of stalls and preemption, at a per-node publish-and-validate. Each algorithm must work out which references are hazardous; Hart et al. know of no upper bound on $K$ for general tree or graph traversals.

Do not benchmark a reclamation scheme with one thread on an idle machine. The cost differences that matter, garbage growth under preemption and fence cost on long traversals, only appear with oversubscribed threads, update-heavy workloads and long data structures.

Grace periods (EBR, RCU) make reads cheap but let one stalled reader block all reclamation. Hazard pointers bound garbage at N x R but charge every visited node. Pick by read pattern and by how much you trust threads to keep moving.

blocks.question: A user-space service runs 200 threads on 16 cores and frequently preempts threads mid-operation. Updates are frequent and memory is tight. Which scheme fits best?
options: Classic QSBR, because reads are free
Hazard pointers, because garbage stays bounded even when threads are preempted
EBR, because pinning is cheaper than a fence per node
No reclamation, because the process restarts nightly
blocks.explain: Oversubscription means many threads are descheduled mid-operation. Under EBR or QSBR any one of them stalls all reclamation, and Hart et al. showed that preemption plus write-heavy workloads can make QSBR and EBR exhaust memory. Hazard pointers cap the backlog at N x R.

blocks.question: A kernel subsystem keeps a routing table read millions of times per second and updated a few times per minute. Readers never sleep while holding entries. What is the best choice?
options: Hazard pointers on every table entry
A reader-writer lock
Reference counting each entry
RCU: readers use rcu_read_lock, updaters publish a copy and free with call_rcu or kfree_rcu
blocks.explain: This is RCU's design point: read-mostly data, non-sleeping readers and natural quiescent states. Readers make no shared writes, while hazard pointers would fence per visited entry and a reader-writer lock makes every reader write to the lock word. Rare updates make the grace-period wait cheap.

blocks.question: A Rust program uses crossbeam-epoch. Memory grows steadily, and a profiler shows one thread blocked on a channel receive inside a function that holds an `epoch::Guard`. What fixes it?
options: Increase the bag size from 64
Drop the guard (or call repin) before blocking on the channel
Switch the CAS to SeqCst ordering
Call `pin()` more often on other threads
blocks.explain: The blocked thread stays pinned in an old epoch, so the global epoch cannot advance past it and every thread's garbage waits. Bag size and memory ordering do not change that. Holding guards only for short, non-blocking sections is the rule for any grace-period scheme.

sources.label: Hart, McKenney, Brown: Making Lockless Synchronization Fast (PDF)
